Tropical Weather Outlook

For the North Atlantic...Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of America:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on newly formed
Tropical Depression Nine, located in the southwestern Gulf of
America.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected during the next 7 days.

item.title: Tropical Depression Nine Public Advisory Number 2
item.description:
Issued at 1000 PM CDT Tue Oct 06 2026 
000
WTNT34 KNHC 070254
TCPAT4
 
BULLETIN
Tropical Depression Nine Advisory Number   2
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL092026
1000 PM CDT Tue Oct 06 2026
 
...TROPICAL DEPRESSION FORECAST TO QUICKLY STRENGTHEN...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 1000 PM CDT...0300 UTC...INFORMATION
-----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...22.1N 95.0W
ABOUT 345 MI...555 KM W OF PROGRESO MEXICO
ABOUT 605 MI...975 KM SW OF THE MOUTH OF THE MISSISSIPPI RIVER
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...35 MPH...55 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...E OR 80 DEGREES AT 5 MPH...7 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...1005 MB...29.68 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
Interests in the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico and the U.S. northern
Gulf Coast should closely monitor the progress of this system.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 1000 PM CDT (0300 UTC), the center of Tropical Depression Nine 
was located near latitude 22.1 North, longitude 95.0 West. The 
depression is moving toward the east near 5 mph (7 km/h). An 
east-northwestward motion is expected on Wednesday, followed by a 
turn toward the northeast and north on Thursday and Friday. On the 
forecast track, the depression is expected to pass to the north of 
the Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday and approach the U.S. northern 
Gulf Coast on Friday.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 35 mph (55 km/h) with higher gusts. 
Steady strengthening is forecast, and the depression is expected to 
become a tropical storm early Wednesday and a hurricane on Thursday.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 1005 mb (29.68 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
Key messages for Tropical Depression Nine can be found in the
Tropical Cyclone Discussion under AWIPS header MIATCDAT4 and WMO
header WTNT44 KNHC.
 
RAINFALL: Tropical Depression Nine is expected to produce rainfall
amounts of 2 to 4 inches through Thursday across coastal portions of
the Bay of Campeche with isolated higher amounts possible in the
states of Campeche and western Yucatan.
 
From Friday through the weekend, the system is expected to produce
rainfall amounts of 3 to 6 inches, with localized totals up to 10
inches, across the central U.S. Gulf Coast extending from
southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Flash and urban
flooding, along with isolated river flooding, will be possible.
 
For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with
Tropical Depression Nine, please see the National Weather Service
Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at
hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?rainqpf and the Flash Flood Risk
graphic at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ero.
 
WIND: Gusty winds are possible in portions of the Yucatan Peninsula
on Thursday.
 
SURF: Swells are expected to affect the western and northern
portions of the Yucatan Peninsula beginning on Thursday and spread
northward toward the Gulf Coast late this week. These swells are
likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.
Please consult products from your local weather office.
 
A depiction of rip current risk for the United States can be found
at: hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ripCurrents
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 400 AM CDT.
 
$$
Forecaster Reinhart

item.title: Tropical Depression Nine Forecast Discussion Number 2
item.description:
Issued at 1000 PM CDT Tue Oct 06 2026 
000
WTNT44 KNHC 070255
TCDAT4
 
Tropical Depression Nine Discussion Number   2
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL092026
1000 PM CDT Tue Oct 06 2026
 
The convective organization of the depression has not changed much 
since the prior advisory. Much of the associated deep convection is 
displaced slightly to the north of the estimated surface center, but 
recently a new convective burst has emerged closer to this location. 
The initial intensity is held at 30 kt for now, consistent with the 
latest T2.0 Dvorak classification from TAFB. An ASCAT-C pass is 
expected to arrive shortly after this advisory issuance and will be 
helpful in reassessing the position and intensity of the system.

The depression is moving slowly eastward (080/4 kt) within weak 
steering currents to the south of an upper trough over the 
southeastern United States. The track models are in good agreement 
that the system should move eastward to east-northeastward through 
Thursday while passing to the north of the Yucatan Peninsula. While 
the center is forecast to remain well offshore, its passage will 
likely produce gusty winds and heavy rainfall for portions of the 
Yucatan Peninsula. A turn toward the northeast and north is 
predicted by Friday as the system moves within the flow between a 
shortwave trough over Texas and a strengthening ridge over the 
western Atlantic. There remains significant along- and cross-track 
spread in the track guidance regarding this northward turn, with the 
AI-based models on the right side of the envelope and generally 
faster than the physics-based guidance. The updated NHC forecast is 
slower than the previous one from 48-96 h to bring it closer to the 
latest corrected consensus (HCCA), but remains on the fast and right 
side of the latest models. Users should closely monitor forecast 
updates given the below-average confidence in this forecast.

High oceanic heat content, moist mid-levels, and upper-level 
divergence should allow the compact system to intensify during the 
next few days. The only limiting factor appears to be southwesterly 
vertical wind shear, which is forecast to strengthen later this week 
as the system approaches the northern Gulf Coast. Most skillful 
models show the system becoming a hurricane over the central Gulf, 
and the latest forecast shows a similar rate of intensification and 
peak intensity as the prior forecast, generally following the more 
aggressive Google DeepMind and HCCA aids. Due to strong shear, it is 
likely that the system peaks in strength before reaching the coast 
as a hurricane. The cyclone is also expected to grow in size as it 
approaches the northern Gulf Coast, and the anticipated convective 
and motion asymmetries will likely cause rain and wind impacts to 
extend far from the center on the eastern side of the storm.

 
Key Messages:
 
1. There is an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge
impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast, and watches could
be required on Wednesday. Residents from Louisiana to the Florida
Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and
ensure they have their hurricane plan in place.
 
2. The system will bring areas of heavy rainfall to the central U.S. 
Gulf coast Friday into the weekend. Flash and urban flooding, along 
with isolated river flooding, will be possible.
 
3. Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico: The depression is expected to
strengthen and could bring gusty winds and areas of heavy rain to
the western portion of the Yucatan Peninsula in a couple of days.
